name: Karl Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Karl. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me the public line and what you really think. What's a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls on the claims line for a regional car insurer. Someone's had a bump on the roundabout, or their windscreen's cracked, and I take the details, check the policy and book the repair. I've been there just under a year. Before that I worked in a warehouse, so sitting at a desk all day is still strange to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when someone's shaken up after a crash and I can tell them the car's booked in and a courtesy car is coming. That feels like doing right by people. The hard part is the claims system, there are about nine screens and I'm a slow typist, so my calls run long. My supervisor's patient with me, but I can tell my numbers are near the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope. Leave things as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, a real person still matters when you've just written your car off. I'd say it at work, and to my dad at Sunday lunch. I'm not on social media much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, because I'm slow and the firm keeps an eye on numbers. Even small things, like the system filling in the claim form for us, mean they expect more calls an hour. I'm the one who'd struggle with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and practise my typing at home, maybe one of those free typing games. I'd keep putting money aside, I've got about two months' worth. I'd stay off the AI stuff unless they made us use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm never fully relaxed about that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're never fully relaxed about that job. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the lads have college diplomas. I came from a warehouse and I don't have the qualifications most of the other agents have. I feel like I'm there on probation forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting my numbers to the middle of the table. And maybe an engagement ring on my girlfriend Anna's finger, so I've got something steady at home too. Stability, that's all I want.

say: I'd say a **real person** still matters after a car crash.
I'd say it at work and at **Sunday lunch** with my dad.
think: Even small automation raises the **calls-an-hour** target.
As a **slow typist**, I'd struggle with tighter targets.
My numbers are already near the **bottom** of the team.
do: Practise **typing at home** with free typing games.
Keep adding to his **two months** of savings.
feel: **Uneasy**, never fully relaxed in the job.
S0.quote: I came from a warehouse and I don't have the qualifications most of the other agents have. I feel like I'm there on probation forever.
fieldNote: He feels like an **outsider** at a desk job, which shapes every answer.
His dream is **stability**: steady numbers and an engagement.
He links even small automation to **higher targets**.

steps.text: Practise typing at home with free online typing games
Keep adding to his two months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers, booking repairs, checking. That's all of my job right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have every right to cut costs, that's how the market works. But I'd also say a firm should look after loyal staff. At church I'd probably ask people to keep an eye out for jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished there in a couple of years. The new ones and the slow ones go first, and I'm both. I'm not a computer person, so learning the new system isn't my way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing Saturdays at my dad's garage again, like I did at school, to keep my hands in. I'd save harder and stop the car upgrade I was planning. I'd look at jobs with my hands, like tyre fitting or parts counters, because there are a few of those around town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Lying awake worried, some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have every right to cut costs. Does that change when it's you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I still think that. I don't want the government paying me to sit at home. I just want to find the next job, and family's where you go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come and work for me, but the garage only makes enough for him and one other guy. He'd find me something though, he always does.

say: I'd say firms have **every right** to cut costs in a market.
I'd ask people at **church** to watch for jobs.
think: The **new and slow** go first, and I'm both.

I'm **not a computer person**, so I'd look to my hands.
do: Work **Saturdays** at his dad's garage again.
Cancel the planned **car upgrade** and save harder.
Look at **tyre fitting** or parts counter jobs in town.
S1.quote: I don't want the government paying me to sit at home. I just want to find the next job, and family's where you go first.
fieldNote: His **free-market** view holds even when it hurts him.
**Family**, not government, is his safety net.
He expects to be **cut early** and plans a hands-on move.

steps.text: Work Saturdays at his dad's car repair garage
Cancel the planned car upgrade and save the money
Apply for tyre fitting or parts counter jobs in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick. That's before I've even finished my probation, the way it feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened, so we deal with it. No moaning. I'd tell the lads at church we need to look after each other, find each other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job's gone within a year or two. Thinking work goes first, and robots don't come for car repairs until about 2031. So the garage gives me three years, maybe more, because people trust a mechanic they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time at the garage as an apprentice, even on less money. I'd cut the gym and the takeaways. Anna and I were going to get engaged next year, and I'd want to wait until I knew what I was earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but also oddly relieved. Like I'm going back to where I belong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relieved. Can you explain that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never felt right at a desk. Under a car, I know what I'm doing. If it takes a crisis to send me back, maybe that's not all bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the engagement. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Anna I want to do it properly, with a ring I've paid for. She'd say she doesn't care about the ring. But I care, so we'd wait a year.

say: I'd say it's happened, so **we deal with it**.
I'd tell people at church to **find each other work**.
think: My **desk job** goes within a year or two.
Car repairs buy **three years or more** before robots.
do: Join his dad's garage **full time** as an apprentice.
Delay **getting engaged** until his income settles.
feel: **Alarmed**, but oddly **relieved** to return to hands-on work.
S2.quote: I never felt right at a desk. Under a car, I know what I'm doing.
fieldNote: The fast scenario pushes him **back to the garage**, which he half wants.
He uses the **robot delay** sensibly to judge his safe years.
Pride shapes his **engagement** timing: he wants to pay for the ring.

steps.text: Join his dad's garage full time as an apprentice
Cancel the gym and stop takeaways
Delay the engagement to Anna by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. A man can plan in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to learn a trade, and young people should be doing apprenticeships, not degrees. I'd say that loudly. I've always thought that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd last two or three years at the insurer, then it goes. That's enough time to get a proper mechanic's qualification. Robots for hands-on work wouldn't come until about 2034, so I'd get a good run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer while it lasts and do the evening motor vehicle course at the college. I'd keep doing Saturdays at the garage. I'd save what I can, aiming for four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like a long job than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not try the new AI tools at the insurer to stay longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it doesn't help in the end. Why spend two years learning something that's gone by 2031? I'd rather learn engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you get engaged in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Five years is enough. I'd want Anna to know I have a plan, and the plan is the garage.

say: I'd say young people should do **apprenticeships**, not degrees.
I'd say there's **time to learn** a trade.
I'd say it **loudly**, because I've always thought it.
think: I'd last **two or three years** at the insurer.
A **mechanic's qualification** gives a good run before 2034.
do: Stay at the insurer and take the **evening motor vehicle** course.
feel: **Anxious**, but it feels like a **long job**, not a fire.
S3.quote: Why spend two years learning something that's gone by 2031? I'd rather learn engines.
fieldNote: He rejects AI tools on **practical grounds**, not just habit.
Five years lets him go ahead with the **engagement**.

steps.text: Take the evening motor vehicle course at the college

Get engaged to Anna once the garage plan is set

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so don't panic. I'd tell younger lads at church to pick a trade now. I'd say the market will sort a lot of it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay at the insurer and do Saturdays at the garage. I'd only make the jump when it's obvious. Ten years is long enough that I'd wonder if it's even true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and my Saturdays, and propose to Anna next year as planned. I'd save steadily. If I saw the insurer cutting claims staff, I'd start the mechanic's course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the sign that it's obvious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my supervisor got moved off the phones. He's been there fifteen years. If they don't need him, they don't need any of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does waiting worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My dad says you should always fix the leak before the rain. But I also don't want to throw away a steady job on a guess.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time**, so don't panic.
I'd say the **market** will sort a lot of it out.
think: Ten years makes me **wonder if it's true** at all.
Until then I'd keep the insurer job and my **garage Saturdays**.
do: Keep the insurer job and **Saturdays** at the garage.

fieldNote: With ten years he **waits for proof**, true to his resistant style.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to leave a steady job before I'm ready. What would help is apprenticeships open to older lads like me, paid properly, so I could learn the trade without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family. Everyone talks about government help, but most people I know would go to their family first. My dad's garage is my plan, not a government scheme.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about government help, but most people I know would go to their family first.
portrait: Karl is 27 and works the **claims line** at a regional car insurer after years in a warehouse.
He's a **slow typist** and feels like he's always on probation.
He **avoids AI tools** and sees his future under a car at his dad's **garage**.
He holds **free-market** views and prefers family help over government.
His plans for **engagement** shift with how fast the change comes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have to leave a steady job before he's ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** open to people in their late twenties.
